title: About
text:
What. MHDSR (Methods in Health Data Science with R) is a live, cohort-based training pathway in applied biostatistics, machine learning, evidence synthesis, and agentic data science, taught in R with reproducible Quarto workflows. It comprises four courses, BIOSTATR, ML4HOR, METAR, and AGENTR, that can be taken independently or followed as a complete pathway.








Figure 1: The MHDSR pathway




Each course can be taken independently (no prerequisite is mandatory), but the order above is recommended for participants building comprehensive mastery.


 Why
Health researchers are often taught statistics and R as separate subjects, disconnected from the reproducible workflows expected in publication and clinical practice. MHDSR closes that gap: every course pairs the underlying methodology with a hands-on R implementation and ends with a reproducible Quarto report.


 Who it’s for
Clinicians, researchers, PhD students, public health professionals, and analysts who want a rigorous, hands-on introduction to modern health data analysis in R. No advanced statistics background is required for BIOSTATR; the other three courses build on it but can be taken independently.


 What you get
Live sessions, slides, notebooks, datasets, and exercises for every session, with direct feedback in a small cohort, ending in a short reproducible Quarto mini-project.

title: METAR
text:
METAR


Conducting Meta-Analysis with REvidence synthesis



 16 hours · 8 sessions  05/10 – 18/10/2026





Course description
METAR provides a practical and methodologically rigorous introduction to conducting meta-analysis with R. It covers the complete evidence-synthesis workflow: formulating a review question, developing an analysis-ready extraction table, computing effect sizes, fitting fixed-effect and random-effects models, assessing heterogeneity, producing forest plots, exploring moderators, assessing publication bias, evaluating certainty of evidence, and preparing a reproducible Quarto report.
The course emphasizes transparent reporting, correct interpretation of pooled estimates, reproducible analysis, and publication-quality tables and figures.


Learning objectives
By the end of METAR, participants will be able to:

formulate a meta-analysis question using the PICO framework;
structure extracted study data for analysis in R;
compute effect sizes for binary and continuous outcomes;
fit fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analysis models;
quantify and explore heterogeneity using Q, I², and tau²;
produce publication-quality forest plots;
conduct subgroup analysis and meta-regression;
assess small-study effects and publication bias;
summarize risk of bias and certainty of evidence;
produce a reproducible meta-analysis report with Quarto.

title: BIOSTATR
text:
BIOSTATR


Applied Biostatistics with RFoundations



 16 hours · 8 sessions  07/09 – 20/09/2026





Course description
BIOSTATR is the entry point of the MHDSR pathway: a practical, rigorous introduction to applied biostatistics for health research using R. It gives participants the foundations everyone else builds on (study design, descriptive statistics, inference, regression, survival analysis, and reproducible reporting) before they move on to ML4HOR, METAR, or AGENTR.
The course emphasizes estimation, interpretation, reproducibility, and appropriate use of statistical methods in clinical research.


Learning objectives
By the end of BIOSTATR, participants will be able to:

formulate health research questions in statistical terms;
identify study designs and variable types;
organize reproducible analyses using R and Quarto;
summarize and visualize health data appropriately;
interpret confidence intervals, p-values, and effect estimates;
compare groups using suitable statistical tests;
fit and interpret linear and logistic regression models;
understand the basics of survival analysis and diagnostic accuracy;
recognize issues related to missing data and causal thinking;
produce a reproducible statistical report.





Schedule



No.


Topic




1


Introduction to biostatistics, study design & reproducible R/Quarto workflow




2


Descriptive statistics & data visualization




3


Estimation, statistical inference & group comparisons




4


Correlation and linear regression




5


Logistic regression and GLMs




6


Survival analysis and diagnostic accuracy




7


Missing data, causal thinking, sample size & reporting




8


Final synthesis and mini-project

Health researchers, clinicians, students with no statistics background required

None; R/RStudio setup covered in Session 1

title: MHDSR
text:
Programme design
The MHDSR pathway takes participants from applied biostatistics through prediction, evidence synthesis, and agentic data science. BIOSTATR gives the foundations: study design, descriptive statistics, inference, regression, survival basics, and reproducible R/Quarto workflows. ML4HOR builds on it with prediction across classification, regression, and time-to-event outcomes, validation, and interpretability. METAR adds evidence synthesis and pooled inference across studies. AGENTR closes the pathway with agentic data science: building and running reproducible analysis pipelines with LLMs and coding agents.
Each course can be taken independently (no prerequisite is mandatory), but the order above is recommended for participants building comprehensive mastery.
BIOSTATR → ML4HOR → METAR → AGENTR. Browse the full catalogue and schedule →

title: ML4HOR
text:
ML4HOR


Machine Learning for Health Outcomes with RPrediction



 16 hours · 8 sessions  21/09 – 04/10/2026





Course description
ML4HOR provides a practical introduction to machine learning for health outcomes research using R. The course covers the complete supervised learning workflow across classification, regression, and time-to-event (survival) outcomes, and explores clustering as a final extension for patient phenotyping, subgroup discovery, and exploratory health-data analysis.
The course emphasizes validation, data leakage prevention, appropriate performance metrics (including censoring-aware metrics for survival), calibration, interpretability, clinical relevance, and reproducible reporting.


Learning objectives
By the end of ML4HOR, participants will be able to:

formulate machine learning questions in health outcomes research;
prepare tabular health datasets for ML analysis;
fit supervised learners for classification, regression, and time-to-event (survival) outcomes;
evaluate models using resampling-based validation and censoring-aware metrics;
tune and compare learners fairly;
assess discrimination, calibration, and clinical usefulness;
interpret ML models using global and local explanation methods;
apply clustering for patient phenotyping and subgroup discovery;
distinguish prediction, clustering, and causal estimation;
produce a reproducible ML report with Quarto.

title: AGENTR
text:
AGENTR


Agentic Data Science with RAgentic workflows



 16 hours · 8 sessions  19/10 – 01/11/2026





Course description
AGENTR is the capstone of the MHDSR pathway: a practical, hands-on introduction to agentic data science, using large language models and coding agents to build, run, and reproduce data analysis pipelines in R from the command line. It builds directly on the R foundations of the earlier courses, and a working knowledge of R is required to get full value from it.
The course works through the full agentic workflow: choosing between frontier and local models, prompting and context engineering, calling R and shell tools from an agent via structured tool use, grounding output with retrieval over data and documents, packaging reusable skills and multi-step agent workflows, and evaluating agent output with tests, guardrails, and human review.
The emphasis throughout is on keeping the analyst in control: verification, provenance, cost, privacy, and honest reporting of AI-assisted work.


Learning objectives
By the end of AGENTR, participants will be able to:

describe what agentic systems are, and where they help or fail in data science;
set up a CLI-based agentic workflow for R projects (API keys, local runtimes, project scaffolding);
compare frontier and local LLMs on capability, cost, latency, and privacy;
write effective prompts and manage context for data analysis tasks;
call R functions and external tools from a model using structured tool use / function calling;
build retrieval over datasets, codebases, and documents to ground model output;
package reusable skills and multi-step agent workflows for recurring analyses;
evaluate agent output with tests and human review, and add guardrails;
manage reproducibility, provenance, cost, and data governance of AI-assisted analyses;
deliver a reproducible, agent-assisted analysis pipeline with an audit trail.





Schedule



No.


Topic




1

3

5

6

7
